title: Employees Assigned to Multiple Departments
description:
Find employees who are assigned to **more than one department**. Return their employee ID, name, and the count of departments they belong to.

**Table: employee_departments** — `id`, `employee_id`, `employee_name`, `department`

Output columns: `employee_id`, `employee_name`, `dept_count`. Order by `employee_id`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE employee_departments (id INTEGER, employee_id INTEGER, employee_name VARCHAR, department VARCHAR); INSERT INTO employee_departments VALUES (1,1,'Alice','Engineering'),(2,1,'Alice','Product'),(3,2,'Bob','Engineering'),(4,3,'Charlie','Marketing'),(5,3,'Charlie','Sales'),(6,3,'Charlie','Product'),(7,4,'Diana','HR'),(8,5,'Eve','Finance'),(9,5,'Eve','HR'),(10,6,'Frank','Sales');
solution_sql: SELECT employee_id, employee_name, COUNT(DISTINCT department) AS dept_count FROM employee_departments GROUP BY employee_id, employee_name HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT department) > 1 ORDER BY employee_id;

test_cases.description: Alice (2 depts: Engineering, Product), Charlie (3 depts: Marketing, Sales, Product), Eve (2 depts: Finance, HR) — 3 employees

hints: GROUP BY employee_id and employee_name, then apply HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT department) > 1.
Use COUNT(DISTINCT department) rather than COUNT(*) to handle any accidental duplicate rows correctly.
Bob, Diana, and Frank each belong to exactly one department and are excluded.
explanation: Alice appears in Engineering and Product → dept_count = 2 ✓. Bob appears only in Engineering → 1, excluded. Charlie appears in Marketing, Sales, Product → dept_count = 3 ✓. Diana is only in HR → 1. Eve is in Finance and HR → dept_count = 2 ✓. Frank is only in Sales → 1. Three employees qualify.
